text: Most of every moulding cycle is spent waiting for the part to cool.
Here's how the mould gets rid of the heat.
Water channels are drilled through the mould plates, close to the cavity.
Baffles and bubblers carry water deep into the cores.
Hot plastic heats the steel, and the water carries that heat away.
Flow is everything. Fast, turbulent water strips heat from the wall. Slow, smooth flow barely touches it.
So each circuit needs enough flow, and the water should come back only a few degrees warmer.
Over time, scale coats the channels.
A thin layer insulates the steel, and the flow gets smaller and smaller.
Rust and dirt block the baffles completely, and O-rings start to leak.
The mould runs hot in spots. Parts warp, sink marks appear, and cycle time creeps up.
Warning signs: low flow on a circuit, a big temperature rise from in to out, hot spots on a thermal camera, and longer cycles.
So: treat the water at the source.
Measure the flow on every circuit, and log it.
Descale the circuits: flush with descaler, neutralise, rinse, and blow them dry.
Pressure test for leaks, replace the O-rings, and label every in and out.
